14.01.title: Technical drawing fundamentals
14.01.html:
A technical drawing is a contract. The machinist in Denpasar or Winterthur who makes your part has never seen your 3D model; they work from views and dimensions. Before learning CAD software, it pays to understand what a drawing view actually is: a projection, and a projection is a linear map.

Orthographic projection

Imagine looking at a part from infinitely far away, so all sight lines are parallel. Each point (x,y,z) lands on the drawing at a position that is a linear function of its coordinates. For the three principal views, the map simply drops one coordinate:

front: (uv​)=(10​00​01​)​xyz​​,top: (10​01​00​),side: (00​10​01​).

Embedded back in 3D, each is a projection matrix P=MTM with P2=P: projecting twice changes nothing. Every edge parallel to the viewing direction collapses to a point, and edges at different depths can land on top of each other. That is why one view is never enough, and why drawings show hidden edges as dashed lines.

Arranging the views

The views are laid out so that they share dimensions: the front and top views share widths, the front and side views share heights. Europe (ISO, including Switzerland) uses first-angle projection: the top view goes below the front view and the left-side view goes on the right. North America uses third-angle, the mirror arrangement. A small truncated-cone symbol in the title block says which one a drawing uses.

Isometric views

A pictorial view rotates the part before projecting. Turn it 45° about the vertical, tilt it by arctan(1/2​)=35.264°, then drop the depth axis. All three axes are then foreshortened equally, by 2/3​=0.8165, which is what “isometric” (equal measure) means.

Worked exampleViews of a stepped block

A block 60 mm long (x), 40 mm deep (y) and 30 mm high (z), with a 25 × 15 mm step cut from the top right along its full depth. Its wireframe has 12 vertices and 18 edges.

  1. Projecting all 18 edges with the front matrix gives 6 distinct segments: the L-shaped outline. The 6 depth edges collapse to points and the back profile lands exactly on the front one.
  2. The top view gives 7 segments: the 60 × 40 rectangle plus a line at x=35 where the step’s vertical face is seen edge-on.
  3. The side view gives 7 segments: the 40 × 30 rectangle plus a line at z=15, the edge of the step.
  4. Each set matches the hand-drawn view exactly, once collinear segments are split at shared vertices.
  5. The isometric matrix foreshortens all three axes by 0.816497 =2/3​.

Exercise 1A block with a slot

A block 80 × 50 × 20 mm has a slot 20 mm wide and 10 mm deep cut through its full depth (y), centred along the top. How many lines does each principal view show (visible and hidden)?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Front view (looking along y): the slot appears as a notch, so the outline has 8 segments, all visible.
  2. Top view: the 80 × 50 rectangle plus two lines at x=30 and x=50, where the slot walls are seen edge-on. Splitting the two long edges at the walls gives 3 pieces each, so 6 + 2 + 2 = 10 minimal segments, all visible.
  3. Side view (looking along x): the 50 × 20 rectangle plus a hidden (dashed) line at z=10, the slot floor, behind the solid end: 5 lines, one of them dashed.

quiz.q: Isometric foreshortening factor √(2/3). 6 decimals.
Isometric tilt angle arctan(1/√2) in degrees. 3 decimals.
How many distinct segments does the front view of the stepped block have?
quiz.explain: Front and back profiles coincide; depth edges collapse.

quiz.q: In first-angle projection (ISO, Europe), the top view is placed:
quiz.explain: First angle: the view is drawn on the far side of the part.

14.02.title: Homogeneous coordinates
14.02.html:
Every time you drag, rotate or place a part in CAD, the software multiplies coordinates by a matrix. Rotation is a 3 × 3 matrix, but translation is not linear: you cannot write “add (50, 0, 0)” as a 3 × 3 matrix product. The trick every CAD kernel and game engine uses is to add a fourth coordinate.

Adding a 1

Write a point as (x,y,z,1). Then rotation and translation together become one 4 × 4 matrix:

​x′y′z′1​​=(R0T​t1​)​xyz1​​=(Rx+t1​).

Directions (vectors) get a 0 in the fourth slot, so translation leaves them alone, exactly as it should.

Rotation about any axis

Rotation by angle θ about a unit axis k is given by Rodrigues' formula, with K the cross-product matrix of k:

R=I+sinθK+(1−cosθ)K2.

R is orthonormal (RTR=I, detR=1), so the inverse of a rigid transform is cheap: (R0​t1​)−1=(RT0​−RTt1​).

Composition and order

Applying A and then B is the single matrix BA. Matrix products do not commute, so order matters: rotating then translating is not translating then rotating. To rotate about a point c instead of the origin, translate c to the origin, rotate, and translate back: T(c)RT(−c).

Worked exampleOrder, a weir gate and a bolt circle

  1. The point (100, 0, 0): rotating 90° about z and then translating by (50, 0, 0) gives (50, 100, 0). Translating first and then rotating gives (0, 150, 0).
  2. A Subak weir gate: a 1.2 m panel hinged at its top edge, at height 1.5 m, swings up 60° about the x axis. With T(c)RT(−c), its bottom edge moves from (0, 0, 0.3) to (0, 1.03923, 0.9). It stays exactly 1.2 m from the hinge, at height 1.5−1.2cos60°=0.9 m.
  3. For a random composition of two rotations and a translation, the cheap rigid inverse equals the general inverse, detR=1, and RTR differs from I by 2×10−16.
  4. Six bolt holes on a 100 mm pitch circle, made by rotating one hole in 60° steps, end up exactly 50 mm apart.

Exercise 1Rotate about a corner

A square plate has corners (0, 0), (2, 0), (2, 2), (0, 2). Rotate it 90° counterclockwise about its corner (2, 0). Where do the corners go? Write the 3 × 3 homogeneous matrix.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. M=T(2,0)R(90°)T(−2,0)=​010​−100​2−21​​.
  2. (0, 0) → (2, −2); (2, 0) → (2, 0), fixed as expected; (2, 2) → (0, 0); (0, 2) → (0, −2).

quiz.q: x-coordinate of (100, 0, 0) after translating by (50, 0, 0) and then rotating 90° about z.
y-coordinate of that point.
Height (m) of the gate’s bottom edge after the 60° swing: hinge at 1.5 m, panel 1.2 m. 2 decimals.

quiz.explain: The first transform sits next to the point.

quiz.explain: So translation does not move it.

14.03.title: "Curves: Bezier and B-splines"
14.03.html:
Draw a smooth curve in any CAD program, a fairing, a fillet, a car body line, and the software stores it not as thousands of points but as a handful of control points and a rule for blending them. The two rules at the heart of every CAD system are the Bezier curve (invented at Renault and Citroën in the 1960s) and its flexible descendant, the B-spline.

Bezier curves

Given control points P0​,…,Pn​, a Bezier curve blends them with the Bernstein polynomials:

B(t)=i=0∑n​(in​)ti(1−t)n−iPi​,0≤t≤1.

The weights are non-negative and sum to 1, so the curve stays inside the convex hull of its control points. It passes through P0​ and Pn​, and its end tangents point along the first and last legs: B′(0)=n(P1​−P0​).

The stable way to evaluate it is de Casteljau’s algorithm: interpolate every leg of the control polygon at fraction t, repeat on the shorter polygon, and stop when one point is left. It uses only linear interpolation, so it never suffers the cancellation that raw polynomials can.

B-splines

A single Bezier curve has two problems: its degree grows with the number of control points, and moving any point changes the whole curve. A B-spline of degree p fixes both by stitching polynomial pieces together at knots u0​≤u1​≤…:

C(u)=i∑​Ni,p​(u)Pi​,Ni,p​(u)=ui+p​−ui​u−ui​​Ni,p−1​(u)+ui+p+1​−ui+1​ui+p+1​−u​Ni+1,p−1​(u).

This is the Cox-de Boor recursion, starting from Ni,0​=1 on [ui​,ui+1​). Each basis function is non-zero only on p+1 knot spans, so moving one control point changes the curve only locally. Repeating the end knots p+1 times (“clamping”) makes the curve start and end at the first and last control points. De Boor’s algorithm is the B-spline version of de Casteljau.

Worked exampleA velomobile nose fairing

A cubic Bezier from the nose tip (0, 0) to the shoulder (600, 250) mm, with inner control points (0, 160) and (300, 250).

  1. De Casteljau and the Bernstein sum agree to 2.3×10−13 mm at 101 values of t. The curve starts at (0, 0) and ends at (600, 250).
  2. A difference quotient at t=0 gives the end tangent (0.001, 480), matching 3(P1​−P0​)=(0,480): the nose leaves the tip straight up, so it is smoothly rounded.
  3. The midpoint B(0.5) is (187.5, 185.0) mm.
  4. A clamped cubic B-spline with 7 control points and knots (0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4): de Boor and the basis-function sum agree to 2.3×10−13; the basis functions sum to 1 within 2.2×10−16; and the curve starts and ends on the end control points.
  5. Moving control point 1 changes the curve only for u between 0.02 and 1.98, inside the support (0, 2) of N1,3​.

Exercise 1By hand

Evaluate the quadratic Bezier with P0​=(0,0), P1​=(2,4), P2​=(4,0) at t=0.25, both with de Casteljau and with Bernstein polynomials.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. De Casteljau: first level (0.5,1) and (2.5,3); second level 0.75(0.5,1)+0.25(2.5,3)=(1.0,1.5).
  2. Bernstein: weights (0.752,2⋅0.25⋅0.75,0.252)=(0.5625,0.375,0.0625), so B=0.375(2,4)+0.0625(4,0)=(1.0,1.5).

quiz.q: Bernstein weight of P₁ in a cubic Bezier at t = 0.5.
y-coordinate of the fairing midpoint B(0.5) for P = (0,0), (0,160), (300,250), (600,250).
How many knot spans does a degree-3 B-spline basis function cover?
A Bezier curve always passes through:
options: Its first and last control points

quiz.q: The main advantage of B-splines over a single high-degree Bezier is:
quiz.explain: Each basis function has small support.

14.04.title: NURBS
14.04.html:
Here is an embarrassing fact about Bezier curves and B-splines: they cannot draw a circle. A polynomial curve can only approximate one. For a CAD system that must model bearing seats, bolt holes and gear blanks to the micrometre, that is not good enough. The fix is to give every control point a weight, which turns the polynomials into ratios of polynomials: NURBS, non-uniform rational B-splines.

Rational curves

C(u)=∑i​Ni,p​(u)wi​∑i​Ni,p​(u)wi​Pi​​.

With all weights equal, this is an ordinary B-spline. Raising wi​ pulls the curve towards Pi​. The neat implementation trick: write each control point in homogeneous coordinates (wi​Pi​,wi​), as in 14.02, run plain de Boor in one dimension higher, and divide by the last coordinate at the end.

A circle, exactly

A rational quadratic Bezier with control points P0​, P1​, P2​ and weights 1,w,1 is always a conic section: an ellipse if w<1, a parabola if w=1, a hyperbola if w>1. For a quarter circle, put P1​ at the corner of the square and choose

w=cos45°=22​​.

Four such quarters, joined with double knots, make a full circle from 9 control points with knots (0,0,0,41​,41​,21​,21​,43​,43​,1,1,1). Every point is exactly on the circle, though the parameter does not advance uniformly in angle. This is how STEP files, Onshape, SolidWorks and FreeCAD’s OpenCascade kernel store circles, cylinders and spheres.

Worked exampleA 62 mm flange

A full NURBS circle of radius 31 mm with 9 control points, weights (1,22​​,1,…) and the double-knot vector above.

  1. At 10001 parameter values, the largest radius error is 1.1×10−14 mm: rounding only.
  2. At u=0.125, the middle of the first quarter, the point sits at exactly 45°. At u=0.0625 it is at 21.5982°, not 22.5°: the speed varies, the shape does not.
  3. The same quarter with w=1 (a plain quadratic Bezier) bulges out to a radius of 32.8805 mm, an error of 1.8805 mm.
  4. The shoulder point at t=21​ lies at radius 29.2271 mm for w=0.5, 31.0000 for w=2​/2, 32.8805 for w=1 and 36.5339 for w=2.

Exercise 1The shoulder point

For the quarter arc P0​=(R,0), P1​=(R,R), P2​=(0,R) with weights (1,w,1), show that the point at t=21​ is at distance R from the origin only when w=2​/2.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At t=21​ the blending weights are 41​,2w​,41​, summing to 21+w​.
  2. The point is (4R​+2wR​, 2wR​+4R​)/21+w​=2(1+w)R(1+2w)​(1,1).
  3. Its distance is 2​R2(1+w)1+2w​. Setting this to R: 2​(1+2w)=2(1+w), so w(22​−2)=2−2​, giving w=2(2​−1)2−2​​=22​​.

quiz.q: Weight of the corner control point for a NURBS quarter circle. 4 decimals.
Radius (mm) of the shoulder point of the w = 1 quarter arc for R = 31. 4 decimals.
How many control points does the 4-arc NURBS circle use (first and last coincide)?

14.05.title: Surfaces
14.05.html:
Curves give edges; parts need skins. A car bonnet, a saddle, the curved roof of a pavilion or the inside of a mould are freeform surfaces. CAD builds them from the same ideas as curves, stretched into two parameters: a surface is a curve of curves.

Tensor-product patches

Take a grid of control points Pij​ and blend in both directions with Bernstein polynomials:

S(u,v)=i=0∑m​j=0∑n​Bim​(u)Bjn​(v)Pij​,0≤u,v≤1.

For m=n=3 this is a bicubic patch with 16 control points. Fixing u gives a Bezier curve in v (an isoparametric line), and vice versa. The patch passes through its 4 corner control points; the boundary curves are the Bezier curves of the boundary rows. B-spline and NURBS surfaces work the same way, with Ni,p​(u)Nj,q​(v) and weights.

Tangents and normals

Differentiating the blending functions gives the tangent vectors Su​=∂S/∂u and Sv​=∂S/∂v. Their cross product is perpendicular to the surface:

n=∥Su​×Sv​∥Su​×Sv​​.

Normals drive shading on screen, offset surfaces (a mould wall of constant thickness), and tool paths for CNC machining, where the cutter must sit exactly one radius away along n. The surface area is ∬∥Su​×Sv​∥dudv.

Worked exampleA saddle roof

A hyperbolic-paraboloid roof, z=xy/25 over −5≤x,y≤5 m. Because the surface is bilinear in u and v, a bicubic patch with control points at the thirds of the square and heights xi​yj​/25 represents it exactly.

  1. Over a 21 × 21 grid of (u,v), the patch matches z=xy/25 to 7×10−16 m. The computed normals match the exact (−y/25,−x/25,1)/∥⋅∥ to 2×10−16, and their lengths are 1 to 1×10−16.
  2. The patch passes through its four corner control points.
  3. At the high corner (5, 5, 1) the normal is (−0.19245,−0.19245,0.96225), tilted 15.7932° from vertical.
  4. The roof area is 101.321155 m² by 12 × 12 Gauss-Legendre integration of ∥Su​×Sv​∥, and 101.321220 m² from 80000 flat triangles. The plan area is 100 m².

Exercise 1A bump in the middle

A flat 4 × 4 control net in the plane z=0 has its four inner control points raised to z=h. How high is the patch at its centre (u,v)=(21​,21​)?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At t=21​ the cubic Bernstein weights are (81​,83​,83​,81​).
  2. Each inner point carries weight 83​⋅83​=649​, so the four together carry 6436​=169​.
  3. The centre height is 169​h: the surface never reaches the inner control points.

quiz.q: Total weight of the four inner control points at the centre of a bicubic patch. 4 decimals.
How many control points does a bicubic patch have?
Tilt (degrees) from vertical of the normal (−0.2, −0.2, 1) normalised. 3 decimals.

quiz.explain: The cross product of the two tangents.

14.06.title: Constructive solid geometry
14.06.html:
A bearing housing is “a block, plus a boss, minus a bore”. That sentence is already a CAD model. Constructive solid geometry (CSG) builds parts from simple primitives combined with booleans: union, intersection and difference. Every CAD program’s “extrude”, “pocket” and “hole” features are booleans underneath.

Signed distance functions

The cleanest way to compute booleans is with a signed distance function (SDF): f(p) is the distance from p to the surface, negative inside and positive outside. For a sphere, f(p)=∥p−c∥−r. For an axis-aligned box with half-sizes h, with q=∣p−c∣−h:

f(p)=∥max(q,0)∥+min(max(qx​,qy​,qz​),0).

The booleans become one-liners:

A∪B=min(fA​,fB​),A∩B=max(fA​,fB​),A∖B=max(fA​,−fB​).

A CSG tree applies these at its nodes; the leaves are primitives. (After a boolean, the result is still negative exactly inside, though no longer an exact distance in every region. For inside/outside tests that does not matter.)

Volume and meshing

With an inside test, volume by Monte Carlo is immediate: sample random points in a bounding box and count. To display or 3D-print the solid we need its surface as triangles. Marching cubes samples f on a grid and places triangles where it changes sign, using a 256-case lookup table. Its table-free cousin, marching tetrahedra, splits each cube into 6 tetrahedra; each tetrahedron has only three cases (1, 2 or 3 corners inside), giving one triangle or two. The mesh volume then follows from the divergence theorem, V=61​∑v0​⋅(v1​×v2​) over consistently oriented triangles.

Worked exampleTwo spheres and a bearing housing

  1. Two spheres of radius 20 mm with centres 24 mm apart. Their overlap is a lens of π(4r+d)(2r−d)2/12=6970.1 mm³, so by inclusion-exclusion the union has volume 2⋅34​πr3−6970.1=60050.5 mm³. Two million Monte Carlo samples of the min-SDF give 60103.5±41.1 mm³, within 1.3 standard errors.
  2. Marching tetrahedra on a 48-cell grid gives 64112 triangles with mesh volume 59965.0 mm³, 0.14% low (flat triangles cut the corners of the curved surface).
  3. A bearing housing: a 60 × 40 × 30 mm block, plus a 40 mm diameter boss 10 mm high, minus a 26 mm bore. Exact volume 63329.2 mm³; Monte Carlo 63362.0±38.2; marching-tetrahedra mesh 63293.5 mm³ from 195908 triangles.

Exercise 1A drilled plate

A 100 × 60 × 10 mm plate has four 8 mm holes drilled through. Write its CSG tree and SDF expression, and its exact volume.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Tree: cut(box, union(hole₁, hole₂, hole₃, hole₄)).
  2. SDF: f=max(fbox​, −min(f1​,f2​,f3​,f4​)), where each fi​ is a cylinder SDF.
  3. Volume: 100⋅60⋅10−4π⋅42⋅10=60000−2010.6=57989.4 mm³.

Signed distance of the point (3, 4, 0) from a sphere of radius 2 at the origin.
Volume (mm³) of the drilled plate. 1 decimal.

14.07.title: Meshes and STL
14.07.html:
CAD kernels think in exact curves and surfaces, but 3D printers, FEM programs and game engines want triangle meshes. The handoff format for 3D printing has been STL since 1987: a bare list of triangles, each with three corner points and a normal. It is simple enough to write from scratch, and simple enough to get subtly wrong.

What a good mesh needs

A mesh is a set of vertices and triangular faces. For a printable solid it must be:

  • Watertight: every edge is shared by exactly two triangles. An edge used once is an open edge, a hole in the skin; an edge used three or more times is non-manifold.
  • Consistently oriented: each triangle lists its corners counterclockwise seen from outside, so its normal n=(v1​−v0​)×(v2​−v0​) points out. Then each edge is traversed once in each direction by its two triangles.

A closed mesh of genus 0 (no through-holes) obeys Euler’s formula V−E+F=2. Its volume follows from the divergence theorem as a sum of signed tetrahedra from the origin:

V=61​faces∑​v0​⋅(v1​×v2​).

If the mesh has holes, this sum depends on where the origin is, which is one way slicers notice broken files.

The STL format

ASCII STL is readable text: facet normal, outer loop, three vertex lines, endloop, endfacet. Binary STL is an 80-byte header, a 4-byte triangle count, then 50 bytes per triangle (12 little-endian floats and a 2-byte attribute). STL stores no connectivity: every triangle repeats its vertices, so a reader must weld equal vertices back together before checking edges. Binary files are about 6 times smaller.

Worked exampleA watch-gear blank

A gear blank of radius 6 mm and thickness 1.2 mm, as a 64-sided prism with fan-triangulated end caps.

  1. 130 vertices, 384 edges, 256 triangles: V−E+F=2. No open edges, consistently oriented.
  2. Volume 135.498895 mm³, exactly the 64-gon prism; the true cylinder is 135.716803 mm³, 0.161% more.
  3. Written as ASCII STL (73571 bytes) and binary STL (12884 bytes =84+50⋅256), then re-read and welded: both give 256 faces on 130 vertices, watertight, with volume 135.498895 and 135.498903 mm³ (binary stores single-precision floats).
  4. Deleting one side triangle leaves 3 open edges. Flipping one keeps the mesh closed, but the orientation check fails.

Exercise 1A cube

A cube is meshed with 2 triangles per face. Find V, E and F, check Euler’s formula, and work out the binary STL size.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. V=8, F=12. Each triangle has 3 edges, each shared by 2 triangles: E=12⋅3/2=18.
  2. V−E+F=8−18+12=2.
  3. Binary size =84+50⋅12=684 bytes.

quiz.q: Binary STL file size (bytes) for 256 triangles.
quiz.explain: 84-byte header and count, 50 bytes per triangle.

quiz.q: Number of edges in a closed triangle mesh with 256 faces.
quiz.explain: Each edge is shared by two faces.

quiz.q: Volume (mm³) of a 64-gon prism, circumradius 6 mm, height 1.2 mm. 4 decimals.
An edge used by only one triangle means:
options: A hole: the mesh is not watertight

quiz.q: Why must an STL reader weld vertices?
quiz.explain: Edges can only be checked after welding.

14.08.title: Parametric sketches and constraints
14.08.html:
In FreeCAD’s Sketcher or Onshape you rough out a shape, then add constraints: this line horizontal, these two perpendicular, this length 80 mm. The sketch snaps into place, and when you drag a point, everything else follows while the constraints hold. Behind that is a nonlinear equation solver, and it is surprisingly small.

Constraints are equations

A 2D sketch with N points has 2N unknowns. Each constraint is an equation r(x)=0:

Constraint Equation
Fix point i at a pi​−a=0 (2 equations)
Distance d ∥pj​−pi​∥2−d2=0
Horizontal yj​−yi​=0
Perpendicular (pj​−pi​)⋅(pl​−pk​)=0
Parallel (pj​−pi​)×(pl​−pk​)=0

Newton’s method

Stack the residuals into r(x) and its Jacobian J=∂r/∂x. A sketch is usually under-constrained while you work, so J is wide and the Newton system has many solutions. Take the minimum-norm step:

Δx=−JT(JJT)−1r=−J+r.

It changes the sketch as little as possible, which is exactly what feels right when you drag: start from the dragged position and Newton pulls it back onto the constraint set nearby. Convergence is quadratic, so a handful of iterations reach 10−12.

Degrees of freedom

The number of remaining degrees of freedom is 2N−rankJ. CAD programs show it (“fully constrained” turns the sketch a different colour). A redundant constraint adds an equation but not rank; a conflicting one makes the system unsolvable. The rank, computed with an SVD, tells them apart from useful constraints.

Worked exampleA plate outline

Four points, corner 0 fixed at the origin, ∣P0​P1​∣=80, ∣P1​P2​∣=50, and three right angles: 8 unknowns, 7 equations.

  1. From a rough sketch, Newton converges in 6 steps to a residual of 3.4×10−13. The rank is 7, so 1 DOF is left: rotation about corner 0.
  2. Adding “P0​P1​ horizontal” leaves 0 DOF; the solution is exactly (0, 0), (80, 0), (80, 50), (0, 50).
  3. Adding ∣P2​P3​∣=80 as well is redundant: 9 equations but rank still 8.
  4. Without the horizontal constraint, dragging corner 2 to (40, 90) and solving takes 8 steps, with residual 9.1×10−13. The plate rotates by 18.3636° and corner 2 lands at (60.1738, 72.6575). The minimum-norm step spreads the change over all the free points, so corner 2 does not end up on the line towards the drag target. Real sketchers treat the drag as a temporary weighted constraint to follow the cursor more closely.
  5. The diagonal stays 802+502​=94.339811321 mm.

Exercise 1Counting DOF

A sketch of a triangle has three points. You fix one point, constrain one side horizontal, and give two side lengths. How many DOF remain? What one constraint would fully define it?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Unknowns: 2⋅3=6. Equations: 2 (fix) + 1 (horizontal) + 2 (lengths) = 5.
  2. If independent, 1 DOF remains: the angle between the two given sides.
  3. A third side length, or an angle, fixes it (in general two mirror solutions exist; the solver picks the one nearest the sketch).

quiz.q: Unknowns in a 2D sketch with 6 points.
Remaining DOF: 4 points, Jacobian rank 7.
Diagonal (mm) of an 80 × 50 rectangle. 6 decimals.
The minimum-norm Newton step is used because:
quiz.explain: Dragging should disturb the sketch minimally.
options: It changes an under-constrained sketch as little as possible
It always finds the global minimum

quiz.explain: It is implied by the others.
options: Adds an equation without adding rank

14.09.title: Parametric part modelling
14.09.html:
A good CAD model is not a shape; it is a recipe. Change the axle standard from quick release to a 12 mm thru-axle and the dropout should update itself: slot wider, walls checked, mass recalculated. That is parametric modelling with design intent, and it is the main reason engineers use CAD instead of drawing tools.

The feature tree

A parametric part is an ordered list of features, each a boolean operation on the result so far:

  1. Sketch the plate outline and pad (extrude) it to thickness t.
  2. Pocket the axle slot, width = axle diameter, open towards the edge.
  3. Drill two frame-bolt holes, spacing from a parameter.
  4. Drill the derailleur-hanger hole.

Each feature refers to parameters, not numbers: slot width =daxle​, bolt positions =±g/2. In FreeCAD these live in a Spreadsheet workbench, in Onshape in “variables”, in SolidWorks in “global variables” or a design table. Change a parameter and the tree rebuilds from the top.

Design intent and rebuild failures

Design intent means the model captures why each dimension is what it is: the slot is centred on the plate axis because the wheel must be; the bolt spacing follows the frame. Rebuilds fail when a parameter change makes a feature impossible (a hole outside the plate) or when the result violates a rule (a wall thinner than the minimum). Robust models check design rules after each rebuild, and a parameter sweep, rebuilding across the whole range of expected values, catches failures before a customer does.

Here we build the tree from scratch with 2D signed distances (14.06) driven by a CSV parameter table, the same structure a FreeCAD spreadsheet gives you.

Worked exampleA 12 mm thru-axle dropout

Parameters from the table: axle 12 mm, plate radius R=16 mm, axle-to-mount L=45 mm, M5 bolts (5.2 mm holes) 14 mm apart, a 10 mm hanger hole, 6 mm thick 6061 aluminium (2.70 g/cm³), minimum wall 4 mm.

  1. Area by counting 0.05 mm grid cells: 1879.26 mm². Exact, from the plate stadium minus the slot (whose straight part ends on the round bottom edge, so it needs ∫R2−x2​dx) and the holes: 1879.28 mm². Mass 30.44 g. No rule violations.
  2. Sweep: axle 10, 12 and 15 mm × R = 16, 18, 20 × L = 40, 45, 50. All 27 rebuilds succeed, every grid area matches the exact formula within 0.6%, and all 27 pass the design rules.
  3. A bad set, R=12 mm with bolts 20 mm apart, is caught: each bolt hole leaves a wall of −0.60 mm, so it breaks out of the plate.

Exercise 1A lighter dropout

With R=16 mm, what is the widest bolt spacing that still leaves a 4 mm wall outside each 5.2 mm hole? And what is the smallest L that keeps 4 mm between the 10 mm hanger hole (at L/2) and a 15 mm axle slot?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Wall =R−g/2−2.6≥4 gives g≤2(16−6.6)=18.8 mm.
  2. Gap =L/2−5−7.5≥4 gives L≥33 mm.

14.10.title: Assemblies and mates
14.10.html:
A bicycle’s rear suspension, a weir-gate lifting linkage, a car’s windscreen wiper: real machines are assemblies of parts that move relative to each other. In CAD, an assembly places parts with mates (Onshape) or joints (FreeCAD Assembly, SolidWorks), and the software works out how they can move. Underneath it is the same constraint solving as in sketches (14.08), one level up.

Bodies and mates

In the plane, each rigid body has 3 coordinates: position (x,y) and angle θ. A point fixed in body k at local position s sits in the world at

p=(xk​yk​​)+(cosθk​sinθk​​−sinθk​cosθk​​)s.

A revolute mate (pin) says two such points coincide: 2 equations. A slider removes 2 as well; a fixed mate removes 3. Counting before solving gives Grübler’s formula for planar mechanisms with n links (including ground) and j pin or slider joints:

M=3(n−1)−2j.

The honest count comes from the rank of the mate Jacobian, as in 14.08: special geometry can make constraints redundant, and the formula cannot see that.

The four-bar

Ground, crank, coupler and rocker: n=4, j=4, so M=1. One input (a motor on the crank) fixes everything. Grashof’s condition says whether the shortest link can turn fully: with shortest s, longest l and the others p, q, it can if s+l≤p+q. Freudenstein’s equation gives the rocker angle in closed form, a check on the numerical assembly.

Worked exampleA crank-rocker

Ground 100 mm, crank 40, coupler 120, rocker 80.

  1. Grashof: s+l=40+120=160≤p+q=180, and the shortest link is the crank, so it turns fully.
  2. Grübler: M=3⋅3−2⋅4=1.
  3. Modelled as 3 bodies (9 unknowns) with 4 pin mates (8 equations), Newton assembles it from a rough guess. The mate Jacobian has rank 8, leaving 1 DOF. Adding a crank drive leaves 0.
  4. Sweeping the crank through 360° in 5° steps, each solve starting from the previous one, the rocker swings between 54.909° and 128.677° (73.768°). It matches Freudenstein’s open-configuration solution to 9×10−16 rad, and every link length is preserved to 10−9 mm.

Exercise 1A window hinge

A casement-window friction hinge is a four-bar with links 20, 50, 40 and 60 mm. Is it Grashof? How many DOF does it have? What if you add a fifth link pinned between the coupler and ground?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. s+l=20+60=80≤p+q=50+40=90: Grashof.
  2. M=3(4−1)−2⋅4=1.
  3. A fifth link adds 1 body and 2 pins: M=3(5−1)−2⋅6=0. It becomes a rigid structure (unless the geometry is special, which only the Jacobian rank reveals).

quiz.q: Grübler mobility of a planar linkage with 6 links (including ground) and 7 pin joints.
Unknowns for 3 moving planar bodies.
Rocker swing (degrees) of the 100/40/120/80 crank-rocker. 3 decimals.
A planar revolute mate removes how many DOF?

quiz.explain: Shortest plus longest at most the sum of the other two.

14.11.title: Scripting CAD
14.11.html:
Clicking through a gear in a GUI is fine once. When you need the whole gear train for a watch movement, 14 wheels and pinions with different tooth counts, writing code that generates each part is faster and repeatable. Tools like CadQuery and build123d (Python on top of the OpenCascade kernel) and OpenSCAD make CAD programmable: the model is a script, version-controlled like any other code.

Programmatic B-rep modelling

A CAD kernel represents solids by their boundary (B-rep): faces bounded by edges bounded by vertices, with exact NURBS geometry underneath. A script builds them with the same operations as the GUI:

A STEP file stores the exact B-rep; STL stores triangles. Re-opening an export and checking that the volume is unchanged is a basic sanity test of any pipeline.

The involute gear

Gear teeth are shaped as involutes of the base circle, the curve traced by the end of a string unwound from it, so that meshing gears roll with a constant speed ratio. For module m (mm per tooth of pitch diameter), z teeth and pressure angle α:

d=mz,db​=dcosα,da​=d+2m,df​=d−2.5m.

A point on the involute at radius r sits at polar angle inv(αr​)=tanαr​−αr​ from where it leaves the base circle, with cosαr​=rb​/r. The tooth thickness on the pitch circle is half the circular pitch, πm/2, which fixes the tooth’s half-angle at the base circle as π/(2z)+inv(α).

Here we write the whole pipeline from scratch: outline, extrusion to a closed mesh, binary STL export and re-import.

Worked exampleA watch wheel

A Swiss-style watch wheel: module 0.15 mm, 60 teeth, 20° pressure angle, 0.25 mm thick.

  1. Pitch diameter 9.0000 mm =mz; base 8.4572, tip 9.3000 and root 8.6250 mm. The outline has 3780 points.
  2. Crossing the outline with the pitch circle, the tooth is 0.235597 mm thick; πm/2=0.235619 mm (the 0.00002 mm gap is the flank discretisation).
  3. Face area 63.293140 mm². The extruded mesh has volume 15.823285 mm³, exactly area × thickness, and the re-opened binary STL (15120 triangles) gives 15.823285 mm³ again.
  4. Rebuilding for 12, 18, 30, 60 and 100 teeth always gives a closed outline with area between the root and tip discs.

Exercise 1A meshing pinion

The 60-tooth wheel drives an 8-leaf pinion (watch “pinions” have few teeth) of the same module. Find the pinion’s pitch diameter, the centre distance and the speed ratio.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Pinion pitch diameter =0.15⋅8=1.20 mm.
  2. Centre distance =(9.00+1.20)/2=5.10 mm.
  3. Ratio =60/8=7.5: the pinion turns 7.5 times per wheel turn. (Real watch pinions use cycloidal, not involute, profiles at such low tooth counts.)

14.12.title: Drawings, GD&T and handoff
14.12.html:
No part is made exactly to size. A drawing must say how far each feature may deviate and still work. Plus-or-minus tolerances on every coordinate are the old way, and they have a flaw you can see with a ruler. Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T, ISO 1101 and ASME Y14.5) states function directly: where a hole must be, how flat a face must be, measured from defined datums.

Datums

A datum reference frame fixes the part the way it will be used: datum A is the face it sits on (3 points of contact), B the edge or bore that locates it (2 points), C what stops it rotating (1 point). Every geometric tolerance names the datums it is measured from, in order: ⊕ ∅0.10 Ⓜ A B C.

Position: square versus round zones

With ±0.1 mm on x and y, a hole’s centre must lie in a 0.2 × 0.2 mm square. But a hole at the square’s corner is 0.12​=0.141 mm off, and the drawing accepts it, so any hole within that distance in any direction would work just as well. A position tolerance uses that round zone directly, diameter 0.22​=0.283 mm, with area

0.22π(0.1414)2​=2π​=1.571

times the square’s: 57% more acceptable parts for the same function. The basic dimensions (boxed, no tolerance) give the true position; the feature control frame gives the zone.

Bonus tolerance and form

The Ⓜ modifier, maximum material condition, says the zone applies when the hole is at its smallest. A bigger hole has more clearance for the bolt, so it may sit further off: allowed position = stated tolerance + (actual size − MMC size). Flatness needs no datum: all points of a face must lie between two parallel planes a distance t apart. The measured value is the minimum zone, which is never larger than the band around a least-squares plane.

The handoff checklist

A complete drawing has: every feature’s size and location (once, no duplicates), datums, tolerances (general ones in the title block, such as ISO 2768-m), material, surface finish where needed, projection symbol, units, revision. FreeCAD’s TechDraw, Onshape drawings and SolidWorks all produce these from the model.

Worked exampleTolerancing the dropout

  1. Zones: the ± 0.1 square is 0.0400 mm²; the round zone through its corners has diameter 0.2828 mm and area 0.0628 mm², 57.1% more.
  2. A CNC that scatters holes with σ=0.045 mm per axis: of 200000 simulated holes, 94.78% pass the square (exact erf2 result 94.82%) and 99.30% pass the round zone (exact 99.28%).
  3. Bonus tolerance for the 5.2 +0.1/0 bolt holes with ∅0.10 at MMC: 0.10 mm at 5.20, 0.15 at 5.25, 0.20 at 5.30.
  4. Flatness of the dropout face from 25 probe points: least-squares band 8.99 µm, minimum zone 8.29 µm. The spec is 50 µm: pass.
  5. A generated SVG drawing carries all 13 required items (slot size, bolt and hanger positions with datums, the 45.0 ± 0.05 axle-to-bolt distance, basic bolt spacing, radius, flatness, material, general tolerance, projection, datums A, B and C). Deleting the bolt spacing is caught by the checklist.

Exercise 1Bonus in practice

A 6.0 +0.2/0 hole has position ∅0.15 Ⓜ. A part measures 6.12 mm with its centre 0.11 mm from true position. Does it pass?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Allowed zone diameter =0.15+(6.12−6.00)=0.27 mm.
  2. The measured centre needs a zone of diameter 2⋅0.11=0.22 mm.
  3. 0.22≤0.27: it passes. Without the Ⓜ modifier (∅0.15 regardless of size) it would fail.
